Chunked Ray Rendering originated as a practical necessity in the early NeRF implementations to handle the memory demands of dense ray sampling during evaluation [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

The claim states that Chunked Ray Rendering originated as a practical necessity to handle memory demands. Source [S1] explicitly mentions wrapping neural network functions to process inputs in smaller chunks 'to manage memory usage during inference'. Source [S2] notes that rays are rendered in smaller batches 'to avoid out-of-memory errors when processing large numbers of rays'. Source [S3] states that frames are rendered by splitting rays into chunks 'to manage GPU memory'. All three sources confirm that the technique is used to handle memory constraints, supporting the claim.

Chunked Ray Rendering is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes large batches of rays in smaller, fixed-size chunks to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors on the GPU [S1, S2, S3, S4, unofficial].

The claim states that Chunked Ray Rendering is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes large batches of rays in smaller, fixed-size chunks to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors on the GPU. Source [S2] explicitly notes that it 'Renders rays in smaller batches to avoid out-of-memory errors when processing large numbers of rays' and defines a 'chunk' as the batch size. Source [S3] notes that it 'Renders frames by splitting rays into chunks to manage GPU memory'. Source [S4] notes it is a 'rendering strategy that processes rays in smaller batches to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors'. All sources confirm the core components of the claim: the technique (chunking/batching rays), the purpose (memory management/preventing OOM), and the context (volume rendering/ray processing).
